items.stem: What does "justify the relevance" of a research question mean?
items.answer: Explain why the question is worth investigating and how it connects to concepts or global issues
items.markingKey: Explain why the question is worth investigating and how it connects to concepts or global issues. Relevance links the inquiry to wider significance.

items.stem: Tomás writes: "Justifying relevance means saying you find the topic interesting." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Relevance must explain the question's significance, for example its links to concepts, a global context or real-world issues.
items.markingKey: Relevance must explain the question's significance, for example its links to concepts, a global context or real-world issues. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a research question and a hypothesis.
items.answer: A research question asks what will be investigated; a hypothesis predicts what the answer might be and can be tested.
items.markingKey: A research question asks what will be investigated; a hypothesis predicts what the answer might be and can be tested. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Source A – Research guide (paraphrased): Paraphrase of a university library guide to developing research questions, 2023

The guide advised students to begin with a broad topic, read widely, and then narrow their focus to a question that is clear, focused, complex and arguable. It suggested testing a question by asking whether it can be answered with the available sources in the time allowed.

How reliable is Source A for someone researching formulating a research question and justifying its relevance (Criterion B)? Justify your answer using its origin and purpose.
items.answer: Origin: Paraphrase of a university library guide to developing research questions, 2023. Purpose: to help students write effective research questions. Value: It gives practical, clear criteria used by experienced researchers. Limitation: It is general advice for university students and is not specific to MYP Individuals and Societies.
items.markingKey: Origin: Paraphrase of a university library guide to developing research questions, 2023. Purpose: to help students write effective research questions. Value: It gives practical, clear criteria used by experienced researchers. Limitation: It is general advice for university students and is not specific to MYP Individuals and Societies. Award up to [3]: origin and purpose identified and USED (not just copied), at least one value and one limitation explicitly linked to them. Reliability is judged for a purpose, not as "biased = useless". MYP I&S criterion D (year 4), scaled to the marks: 7-8 discusses concepts, issues and theories in detail, synthesises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, analyses and evaluates a range of sources in terms of origin and purpose, examining value and limitations, and interprets different perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2 limited, mostly assertion.

items.stem: Using a student inquiry into Mumbai's floods as an example, explain refining a research question.
items.answer: A student began with "Why does it flood?" and refined it to "How did the destruction of mangroves contribute to flooding in Mumbai in July 2005?" Adding place, time and a specific factor made the question focused and researchable.
items.markingKey: Context (A student began with "Why does it flood?" and refined it to "How did the destruction of mangroves contribute to flooding in Mumbai in July 2005?") – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: adding place, time and a specific factor made the question focused and researchable. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to refining a research question.

items.stem: Evaluate the research question "Are trains good?" for an MYP Individuals and Societies investigation into formulating a research question and justifying its relevance (Criterion B). Rewrite it so that it is clear, focused and researchable.
items.answer: Weakness: it is a vague value question Improved: "To what extent did the Delhi Metro reduce traffic congestion in Delhi between 2002 and 2020?"
items.markingKey: 1 mark: weakness identified (it is a vague value question); 1-2 marks: a focused question such as "To what extent did the Delhi Metro reduce traffic congestion in Delhi between 2002 and 2020?" (clear scope – place, period or group – and open, researchable wording); 1 mark: justification of the change. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem:

"A good research question is the most important part of an investigation." Using Source A and your own knowledge, to what extent do you agree?
items.answer: A strong research question is the foundation, but an investigation also depends on effective planning, sources and critical analysis.
items.markingKey: From the source: Narrow a topic to a clear, focused, arguable and researchable question. Own knowledge for: it shapes the sources, methods and argument; a vague question leads to a weak investigation. Own knowledge against: the quality of sources and analysis also matter; a good question can still be undermined by poor planning. items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "A good research question is the most important part of an investigation."
items.answer: A strong research question is the foundation, but an investigation also depends on effective planning, sources and critical analysis.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it shapes the sources, methods and argument; a vague question leads to a weak investigation. Arguments against: the quality of sources and analysis also matter; a good question can still be undermined by poor planning. items.stem: Explain why a good research question is open rather than closed.
items.answer: An open question ("how", "why", "to what extent") requires analysis and evidence, while a closed question can be answered with yes/no or a single fact.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: An open question ("how", "why", "to what extent") requires analysis and evidence, while a closed question can be answered with yes/no or a single fact. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "Once written, a research question cannot be changed." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Researchers often refine their question as they find sources; recording these changes shows good investigating skills.
items.markingKey: Researchers often refine their question as they find sources; recording these changes shows good investigating skills. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

The guide advised students to begin with a broad topic, read widely, and then narrow their focus to a question that is clear, focused, complex and arguable. It suggested testing a question by asking whether it can be answered with the available sources in the time allowed.

Outline the main argument or view that Source A presents, quoting or referring to the source.
items.answer: Narrow a topic to a clear, focused, arguable and researchable question.
items.markingKey: Narrow a topic to a clear, focused, arguable and researchable question. Award 1 mark per relevant point drawn from the source, up to [3]; own knowledge is not credited here. Criterion D: interpreting a source.

items.stem: In MLA style, how is a book usually cited in the text?
options: By the author's surname and page number, e.g. (Tinker 45)
items.answer: By the author's surname and page number, e.g. (Tinker 45)
items.markingKey: D. MLA uses author–page.

items.stem: Nia writes: "Primary sources are always more reliable than secondary sources." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Primary sources can be biased or limited; secondary sources by experts may be more balanced. Reliability depends on origin and purpose.
items.markingKey: Primary sources can be biased or limited; secondary sources by experts may be more balanced. Reliability depends on origin and purpose. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why researchers cite their sources.
items.answer: Citations acknowledge others' work, avoid plagiarism, let readers check the evidence and show the range and quality of research.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Citations acknowledge others' work, avoid plagiarism, let readers check the evidence and show the range and quality of research. (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Using accurate subject terminology and at least one specific example, write a structured paragraph that responds to: Explain why a citation style must be used consistently.
items.answer: Consistency makes references clear and easy to follow and shows academic honesty and accuracy.
items.markingKey: Content: Consistency makes references clear and easy to follow and shows academic honesty and accuracy. Structure: a clear point that answers the question, specific evidence, explanation that links evidence to the point, and a closing link. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: Justify the relevance of the research question "How do primary accounts of the 1943 Bengal famine differ from official British reports?"
items.answer: It compares sources and perspectives, developing source skills.
items.markingKey: It compares sources and perspectives, developing source skills. Award marks for relevance to the unit's concepts or global context, and for showing the question is focused and can be answered with available sources. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Evaluate the research question "What was the Bengal famine?" for an MYP Individuals and Societies investigation into using a range of primary and secondary sources and citing them in MLA and APA format. Rewrite it so that it is clear, focused and researchable.
items.answer: Weakness: it is a descriptive question Improved: "How do primary accounts of the 1943 Bengal famine differ from official British reports?"
items.markingKey: 1 mark: weakness identified (it is a descriptive question); 1-2 marks: a focused question such as "How do primary accounts of the 1943 Bengal famine differ from official British reports?" (clear scope – place, period or group – and open, researchable wording); 1 mark: justification of the change. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "secondary source"?
options: A source that interprets or analyses primary sources, such as a textbook or history book
Checking evidence by comparing it with other independent sources
The American Psychological Association style, often used in social sciences, with author–date in-text citations
Presenting someone else's words or ideas as your own without acknowledgement
items.answer: A source that interprets or analyses primary sources, such as a textbook or history book
items.markingKey: A. "secondary source" is a source that interprets or analyses primary sources, such as a textbook or history book.

items.stem:
Source A – Style guide (paraphrased): Paraphrase of the Publication Manual of the American Psychological Association, 7th edition, 2020

The guide explained that every in-text citation must match an entry in the reference list, which should be arranged alphabetically by author surname and include the author, date, title and source so that readers can find the work.

Explain one value and one limitation of Source A for an investigation into using a range of primary and secondary sources and citing them in MLA and APA format, referring to its origin and purpose.
items.answer: Origin: Paraphrase of the Publication Manual of the American Psychological Association, 7th edition, 2020. Purpose: to set standards for academic writing and citation. Value: It is the official guide to APA style. Limitation: It focuses on format, not on judging the quality of sources.
items.markingKey: Origin: Paraphrase of the Publication Manual of the American Psychological Association, 7th edition, 2020. Purpose: to set standards for academic writing and citation. Value: It is the official guide to APA style. Limitation: It focuses on format, not on judging the quality of sources. items.stem: Formulate an action plan to investigate the research question "How do primary accounts of the 1943 Bengal famine differ from official British reports?" Include the main steps, at least one primary and one secondary source, and how you would record your findings.
items.answer: Collect memoirs, newspaper reports and official documents; compare using OPVL; read two historians; cite in MLA.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Collect memoirs, newspaper reports and official documents; compare using OPVL; read two historians; cite in MLA. Credit: logical sequence of steps with a timeline; varied, appropriate sources (primary and secondary) named specifically; a method for recording and citing information (e.g. a source log in MLA/APA); a step for evaluating the process and results. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: A government report on its own policy may be limited because of what?
options: It may present the policy positively
items.answer: It may present the policy positively
items.markingKey: C. Consider the creator's interests.

items.stem: Explain the difference between usefulness and reliability.
items.answer: Reliability is how accurate and trustworthy a source is; usefulness depends on whether it helps answer the question, which even an unreliable source may do.
items.markingKey: Reliability is how accurate and trustworthy a source is; usefulness depends on whether it helps answer the question, which even an unreliable source may do. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why historians compare several sources.
items.answer: Comparing sources allows evidence to be corroborated, contradictions to be identified and a more balanced conclusion to be reached. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Comparing sources allows evidence to be corroborated, contradictions to be identified and a more balanced conclusion to be reached. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (3 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Which of the following is the most clear and focused research question for an investigation into thinking critically: analysing sources for origin, purpose, value and limitation (Criterion D)?
options: How useful are wartime posters for understanding women's experiences in American factories during the Second World War?
items.answer: How useful are wartime posters for understanding women's experiences in American factories during the Second World War?
items.markingKey: A. It is open, has a clear scope (place/period/group) and can be answered with evidence; the others are too broad, closed or off-topic.

items.stem: A student chose the research question "How useful are wartime posters for understanding women's experiences in American factories during the Second World War?" Explain two reasons why this question is relevant and worth investigating.
items.answer: It develops critical evaluation of sources for a historical question.
items.markingKey: It develops critical evaluation of sources for a historical question. Award marks for relevance to the unit's concepts or global context, and for showing the question is focused and can be answered with available sources. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: Ana is investigating thinking critically: analysing sources for origin, purpose, value and limitation (Criterion D) and proposes the research question: "What is a poster?" Explain one weakness of this research question and write a more focused alternative.
items.answer: Weakness: it is a definition question Improved: "How useful are wartime posters for understanding women's experiences in American factories during the Second World War?"
items.markingKey: 1 mark: weakness identified (it is a definition question); 1-2 marks: a focused question such as "How useful are wartime posters for understanding women's experiences in American factories during the Second World War?" (clear scope – place, period or group – and open, researchable wording); 1 mark: justification of the change. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem:
Source A – Poster (described): J. Howard Miller, poster for Westinghouse Electric, United States, 1943

A colour poster shows a confident woman in a red-and-white headscarf flexing her arm, under the slogan "We Can Do It!". It was produced for a US company's factories to boost workers' morale during the Second World War.

Evaluate Source A as evidence about thinking critically: analysing sources for origin, purpose, value and limitation (Criterion D). Consider its origin, purpose, value and limitations.
items.answer: Origin: J. Howard Miller, poster for Westinghouse Electric, United States, 1943. Purpose: to motivate factory workers and maintain production during the war. Value: It shows how employers encouraged women's war work and how women workers were portrayed. Limitation: It was displayed only briefly within one company at the time; its fame as a feminist symbol dates from the 1980s, so it shows intent rather than workers' experiences.
items.markingKey: Origin: J. Howard Miller, poster for Westinghouse Electric, United States, 1943. Purpose: to motivate factory workers and maintain production during the war. Reliability is judged for a purpose, not as "biased = useless". "Sources produced by governments are less reliable than those produced by individuals." Using Source A and your own knowledge, to what extent do you agree?
items.answer: Reliability depends on the origin, purpose and content of each source, not simply on whether it comes from a government or an individual.
items.markingKey: From the source: Women workers were capable and essential to the war effort. Own knowledge for: governments may present their policies positively or use propaganda; individual accounts can reveal hidden experiences. Own knowledge against: governments often hold the most complete data, such as censuses; individuals may also be biased, mistaken or limited in view. Judgement: Reliability depends on the origin, purpose and content of each source, not simply on whether it comes from a government or an individual. Top answers integrate the source with own knowledge and comment on the source's origin/purpose. MYP I&S criterion D (year 4), scaled to the marks: 7-8 discusses concepts, issues and theories in detail, synthesises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, analyses and evaluates a range of sources in terms of origin and purpose, examining value and limitations, and interprets different perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2 limited, mostly assertion.

items.stem: Explain why historians compare several sources.
items.answer: Comparing sources allows evidence to be corroborated, contradictions to be identified and a more balanced conclusion to be reached.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Comparing sources allows evidence to be corroborated, contradictions to be identified and a more balanced conclusion to be reached. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims: "A biased source is useless." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Biased sources can be valuable evidence of perspectives and attitudes.
items.markingKey: Biased sources can be valuable evidence of perspectives and attitudes. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Nia argues that "Sources produced by governments are less reliable than those produced by individuals." Sofia disagrees. Explain one piece of evidence each student could use, and state which view you find more convincing and why.
items.answer: Reliability depends on the origin, purpose and content of each source, not simply on whether it comes from a government or an individual.
items.markingKey: Nia: governments may present their policies positively or use propaganda. Sofia: governments often hold the most complete data, such as censuses. Judgement (1-2 marks): Reliability depends on the origin, purpose and content of each source, not simply on whether it comes from a government or an individual.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A label or note added to a map, graph or image to explain features"?
items.answer: annotation
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of annotation.

items.stem: Mohammed writes: "A longer answer always gets more marks." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Marks reward relevant, well-organised and supported points; padding can weaken an answer.
items.markingKey: Marks reward relevant, well-organised and supported points; padding can weaken an answer. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between describing and explaining.
items.answer: Describing says what something is like or what happened; explaining gives reasons or causes, showing why or how.
items.markingKey: Describing says what something is like or what happened; explaining gives reasons or causes, showing why or how. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Source A – Speech (paraphrased): Paraphrase of Hans Rosling, TED talk "The best stats you've ever seen", Monterey, California, 2006

The speaker argued that many people hold an outdated view of the world, believing that most countries are poor and have large families. Using animated data on income and life expectancy, he showed that most countries had moved to the middle.

Identify two points that Source A makes about communicating information in structured essays, reports and presentations (Criterion C), using evidence from the source.
items.answer: The world has developed more than many people think.
items.markingKey: The world has developed more than many people think. Award 1 mark per relevant point drawn from the source, up to [2]; own knowledge is not credited here. Criterion D: interpreting a source.

items.stem: With reference to the IPCC "Summary for Policymakers", explain how it illustrates adapting communication to an audience.
items.answer: IPCC assessments include a short summary in plain language with key figures, written for governments rather than scientists. The same research is presented differently for different readers.
items.markingKey: Context (IPCC assessments include a short summary in plain language with key figures, written for governments rather than scientists.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: the same research is presented differently for different readers. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to adapting communication to an audience.

"Visual presentations are more effective than written essays for communicating ideas in Individuals and Societies." Using Source A and your own knowledge, to what extent do you agree?
items.answer: Each format has strengths; the most effective choice depends on the purpose and audience, and many good investigations combine both.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "format"?
options: A sentence stating the main argument of an essay
Presenting someone else's words or ideas as your own without acknowledgement
A particular point of view shaped by a person's position, experience or interests
The type of communication, such as an essay, report, poster, presentation or podcast
items.answer: The type of communication, such as an essay, report, poster, presentation or podcast
items.markingKey: D. "format" is the type of communication, such as an essay, report, poster, presentation or podcast.

items.stem: Suggest and justify the most appropriate graph or map to present data on how pebble size changes with distance downstream. State two features your graph must include.
items.answer: A scatter graph – distance and size are both continuous variables and the trend can be seen
items.markingKey: A scatter graph (1); justification: distance and size are both continuous variables and the trend can be seen (1); features (1): title, labelled axes with units or key, scale, source of data. Criterion C ii.

Explain one value and one limitation of Source A for an investigation into communicating information in structured essays, reports and presentations (Criterion C), referring to its origin and purpose.
items.answer: Origin: Paraphrase of Hans Rosling, TED talk "The best stats you've ever seen", Monterey, California, 2006. Purpose: to challenge misconceptions about global development using data. Value: It shows a powerful way of communicating data to a general audience. Limitation: As a talk designed to engage, it simplifies data and focuses on positive trends.
items.markingKey: Origin: Paraphrase of Hans Rosling, TED talk "The best stats you've ever seen", Monterey, California, 2006. Purpose: to challenge misconceptions about global development using data. items.stem: Which feature makes a research question too broad?
options: It uses a command term such as "to what extent"
It has no limits of place, time or aspect
items.answer: It has no limits of place, time or aspect
items.markingKey: C. Narrow scope makes a question manageable.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A particular point of view shaped by a person's position, experience or interests"?
items.answer: perspective
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of perspective.

items.stem: In APA style, which details appear in an in-text citation?
items.answer: The author's surname and the year of publication
items.markingKey: The author's surname and the year of publication. For example (Yunus, 2006).

items.stem: Briefly explain why graphs must have titles, labels and units.
items.answer: Without them, readers cannot tell what the data show, so the evidence cannot be interpreted or trusted.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Without them, readers cannot tell what the data show, so the evidence cannot be interpreted or trusted. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why a research question should be focused.
items.answer: A focused question can be answered in depth with the time and sources available, leading to a clearer argument and analysis.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: A focused question can be answered in depth with the time and sources available, leading to a clearer argument and analysis. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Freya writes: "A primary source is always reliable because the author was there." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Eyewitnesses may have limited views, faulty memory or reasons to distort what happened.
items.markingKey: Eyewitnesses may have limited views, faulty memory or reasons to distort what happened. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between MLA in-text citation and APA in-text citation.
items.answer: MLA gives the author and page number (Sen 45); APA gives the author and year (Sen, 1981).
items.markingKey: MLA gives the author and page number (Sen 45); APA gives the author and year (Sen, 1981). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why a conclusion should not introduce new evidence.
items.answer: The conclusion answers the question by summarising and weighing the arguments already made; new evidence would need its own analysis.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The conclusion answers the question by summarising and weighing the arguments already made; new evidence would need its own analysis. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why researchers reflect on and revise their research question.
items.answer: Early research may show that a question is too broad, lacks sources or has already been answered, so refining it improves the investigation.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Early research may show that a question is too broad, lacks sources or has already been answered, so refining it improves the investigation. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: The number of women in the US labour force was 12 million in 1940 and 18.6 million in 1945 (approx., US Bureau of Labor Statistics). Calculate the percentage change.
items.markingKey: Percentage change = (new − old) ÷ old × 100 (M1) = (18.6 − 12) ÷ 12 × 100 = +55.0% (A1). Dividing by the new value is a common error.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Gapminder data shows using secondary data sets.
items.answer: The Gapminder Foundation, founded by Hans Rosling, publishes free data on income, health and population for every country, drawing on the UN and World Bank. Reliable compiled data allows students to analyse global trends.
items.markingKey: Context (The Gapminder Foundation, founded by Hans Rosling, publishes free data on income, health and population for every country, drawing on the UN and World Bank.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: reliable compiled data allows students to analyse global trends. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to using secondary data sets.

items.stem: Using accurate subject terminology and at least one specific example, write a structured paragraph that responds to: Explain why communication should be adapted to the audience.
items.answer: Different audiences have different knowledge and needs; language, detail and format must suit them so the message is understood.
items.markingKey: Content: Different audiences have different knowledge and needs; language, detail and format must suit them so the message is understood. Structure: a clear point that answers the question, specific evidence, explanation that links evidence to the point, and a closing link. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: Using accurate subject terminology and at least one specific example, write a structured paragraph that responds to: Explain why researchers write an action plan.
items.answer: It organises tasks, sources and deadlines, ensures the investigation is manageable, and allows progress to be checked and adjusted.
items.markingKey: Content: It organises tasks, sources and deadlines, ensures the investigation is manageable, and allows progress to be checked and adjusted. Structure: a clear point that answers the question, specific evidence, explanation that links evidence to the point, and a closing link. items.stem: The number of women in the US labour force went from 12 million in 1940 to 18.6 million in 1945. Which is the percentage change?
Which of the following is the most clear and focused research question for an investigation into using a range of primary and secondary sources and citing them in MLA and APA format?
options: How do primary accounts of the 1943 Bengal famine differ from official British reports?
items.answer: How do primary accounts of the 1943 Bengal famine differ from official British reports?
items.markingKey: A. It is open, has a clear scope (place/period/group) and can be answered with evidence; the others are too broad, closed or off-topic.

items.stem: Amara argues that "Visual presentations are more effective than written essays for communicating ideas in Individuals and Societies." Maya disagrees. Explain one piece of evidence each student could use, and state which view you find more convincing and why.
items.answer: Each format has strengths; the most effective choice depends on the purpose and audience, and many good investigations combine both.
items.markingKey: Amara: visuals make data and patterns easy to see. Maya: essays allow detailed, nuanced argument and evaluation. Judgement (1-2 marks): Each format has strengths; the most effective choice depends on the purpose and audience, and many good investigations combine both.

items.stem: Plan an extended response to the question: "A good research question is the most important part of an investigation." To what extent do you agree? Give a thesis, two arguments with specific evidence, a counter-argument and a conclusion.
items.answer: Thesis: A strong research question is the foundation, but an investigation also depends on effective planning, sources and critical analysis.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it shapes the sources, methods and argument; a vague question leads to a weak investigation. Counter-arguments: the quality of sources and analysis also matter; a good question can still be undermined by poor planning. Thesis/conclusion: A strong research question is the foundation, but an investigation also depends on effective planning, sources and critical analysis. Credit a thesis that answers the question, logically ordered paragraphs each with specific evidence, a counter-argument that is weighed, and a conclusion that follows. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: Write the introduction and an outline of the body paragraphs for an essay that evaluates the view that "Sources produced by governments are less reliable than those produced by individuals."
items.answer: Thesis: Reliability depends on the origin, purpose and content of each source, not simply on whether it comes from a government or an individual.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: governments may present their policies positively or use propaganda; individual accounts can reveal hidden experiences. Counter-arguments: governments often hold the most complete data, such as censuses; individuals may also be biased, mistaken or limited in view. Thesis/conclusion: Reliability depends on the origin, purpose and content of each source, not simply on whether it comes from a government or an individual. Credit a thesis that answers the question, logically ordered paragraphs each with specific evidence, a counter-argument that is weighed, and a conclusion that follows. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: Plan an extended response to the question: "Primary sources are more valuable than secondary sources for historical investigation." To what extent do you agree? Give a thesis, two arguments with specific evidence, a counter-argument and a conclusion.
items.answer: Thesis: Primary sources are essential evidence, but secondary sources provide context and interpretation; the most valuable investigations use both critically.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: they provide direct evidence from the time; they reveal the views of participants. Counter-arguments: they can be biased, incomplete or hard to interpret without context; secondary sources offer expert analysis of many primary sources. Thesis/conclusion: Primary sources are essential evidence, but secondary sources provide context and interpretation; the most valuable investigations use both critically. Credit a thesis that answers the question, logically ordered paragraphs each with specific evidence, a counter-argument that is weighed, and a conclusion that follows. Criterion C (communicating): appropriate style and register for the purpose, a clear structure suited to the format (topic sentence, developed evidence, explanation, link back to the question), accurate subject terminology, and sources documented with a recognised convention (MLA or APA).

items.stem: "Visual presentations are more effective than written essays for communicating ideas in Individuals and Societies." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Each format has strengths; the most effective choice depends on the purpose and audience, and many good investigations combine both.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: visuals make data and patterns easy to see; presentations can engage wide audiences. Arguments against: essays allow detailed, nuanced argument and evaluation; visuals can oversimplify or mislead. Supported judgement: Each format has strengths; the most effective choice depends on the purpose and audience, and many good investigations combine both. Markbands (12 marks): MYP I&S criterion D (year 4), scaled to the marks: 7-8 discusses concepts, issues and theories in detail, synthesises information to make valid, well-supported arguments, analyses and evaluates a range of sources in terms of origin and purpose, examining value and limitations, and interprets different perspectives and their implications; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate, partly descriptive; 1-2 limited, mostly assertion.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "research question".
items.answer: A clear, focused question that guides an investigation and can be answered with evidence in the time available
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a clear, focused question that guides an investigation and can be answered with evidence in the time available. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "purpose"?
options: An alphabetical list of all sources used in an investigation
A source that interprets or analyses primary sources, such as a textbook or history book
A structured document with headings that presents findings, data and recommendations
Why a source was created and for which audience
items.answer: Why a source was created and for which audience
items.markingKey: D. "purpose" is why a source was created and for which audience.

items.stem: Define the term "secondary source".
items.answer: A source that interprets or analyses primary sources, such as a textbook or history book
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a source that interprets or analyses primary sources, such as a textbook or history book. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between describing and explaining.
items.answer: Describing says what something is like or what happened; explaining gives reasons or causes, showing why or how.
items.markingKey: Describing says what something is like or what happened; explaining gives reasons or causes, showing why or how. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between a research question and a hypothesis.
items.answer: A research question asks what will be investigated; a hypothesis predicts what the answer might be and can be tested.
items.markingKey: A research question asks what will be investigated; a hypothesis predicts what the answer might be and can be tested. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain the difference between reliability and usefulness.
items.answer: Reliability is how accurate and trustworthy a source is; usefulness depends on whether it helps answer the question, which even an unreliable source may do.
items.markingKey: Reliability is how accurate and trustworthy a source is; usefulness depends on whether it helps answer the question, which even an unreliable source may do. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Primary sources are always more reliable than secondary sources." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Primary sources can be biased or limited; secondary sources by experts may be more balanced. Reliability depends on origin and purpose.
items.markingKey: Primary sources can be biased or limited; secondary sources by experts may be more balanced. Reliability depends on origin and purpose. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "Presentations do not need references." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Sources used in presentations must also be acknowledged, for example on slides and in a final reference list.
items.markingKey: Sources used in presentations must also be acknowledged, for example on slides and in a final reference list. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between an open research question and a closed research question.
items.answer: An open question requires analysis and explanation; a closed question can be answered with a single fact or yes/no.
items.markingKey: An open question requires analysis and explanation; a closed question can be answered with a single fact or yes/no. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: You have three weeks to investigate "How useful are wartime posters for understanding women's experiences in American factories during the Second World War?" Outline a step-by-step plan, the sources you would use and one way you would evaluate your process at the end.
items.answer: Collect posters, oral histories and employment data; apply OPVL; compare; reach a judgement; cite in MLA.
items.markingKey: Indicative plan: Collect posters, oral histories and employment data; apply OPVL; compare; reach a judgement; cite in MLA. Credit: logical sequence of steps with a timeline; varied, appropriate sources (primary and secondary) named specifically; a method for recording and citing information (e.g. a source log in MLA/APA); a step for evaluating the process and results. Criterion B (investigating): a clear, focused research question whose relevance is justified, a realistic action plan, appropriate and varied methods/sources, and reflection on the process.

items.stem: You used a book by Alfred W. Crosby called "The Columbian Exchange: Biological and Cultural Consequences of 1492", published by Greenwood in 1972. Write the entry for your bibliography in APA (7th edition) format (write the title in plain text; it would be italicised in a typed document).
items.answer: Crosby, A. W. (1972). The Columbian exchange: Biological and cultural consequences of 1492. Greenwood.
items.markingKey: Crosby, A. W. (1972). The Columbian exchange: Biological and cultural consequences of 1492. Greenwood. 1 mark for correct order of elements (author, title, publisher, date in brackets after the author); 1 mark for punctuation and sentence-case title and initials. Criterion C iii: documenting sources.

items.stem: A student wants to present data on the number of votes won by each party in an election. Which is the most appropriate way to present it?
items.answer: A bar chart
items.markingKey: C. A bar chart: it compares separate categories.

items.answer: Comparing sources allows evidence to be corroborated, contradictions to be identified and a more balanced conclusion to be reached.
items.markingKey: Content: Comparing sources allows evidence to be corroborated, contradictions to be identified and a more balanced conclusion to be reached. items.stem: Noah is investigating communicating information in structured essays, reports and presentations (Criterion C) and proposes the research question: "What is the monsoon?" Explain one weakness of this research question and write a more focused alternative.
items.answer: Weakness: it is a definition question Improved: "How can climate data for Mumbai be presented most effectively to explain monsoon flooding risks to residents?"

items.stem: You have three weeks to investigate "How has the Chipko movement influenced forest policy in Uttarakhand since 1973?" Outline a step-by-step plan, the sources you would use and one way you would evaluate your process at the end.
